new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Spot-checks of the works the folder holds as silent: (1) Goddard 2008 Notes on Mahican : 'Loup B' section pp. 248-249 is about r/l/n reflexes and doublets; all stress remarks (p. 275 'with shifted stress' n. 61; n. 13 'These differences make it difficult to reconstruct the stress rules of Proto-Algonquian') concern Mahican/Munsee/PA, nothing on Loup B stress - silent confirmed. (2) Pentland 2009 Nominal inflection in Nipmuck : pp. 243-244 and n. 16 state PEA final-short-vowel loss 'except when it bore the only stress in the word' and that 'every long vowel and every second short vowel bore a stress' - a PEA/SNEA historical statement, not about Loup B; silent on Loup B stress confirmed (Loup…

sources.citation: Pentland, David H. 2009. Nominal Inflection in Nipmuck. Papers of the 41st Algonquian Conference, 230-267.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: About Loup A (Nipmuck). Mentions Loup B only as the Pocumtuck vocabulary 'in which <r> and <n> predominate' (p. 231) and cites one Loup B word from the manuscript ('ASSM 82, fo. 178', p. 240 n. 9). Its stress remarks are historical (PEA final-vowel loss 'except when it bore the only stress in the word', p. 243; n. 16 p. 244 on 'every long vowel and every second short vowel bore a stress') and not a Loup B rule.

sources.citation: Gustafson, Holly Suzanne. 2000. A Grammar of the Nipmuck Language. MA thesis, University of Manitoba (Loup A, Mathevet's Mots loups).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Not Loup B (it is the loup1243 source already held and checked), but it is the only 'Loup' work with an explicit stress inference (PA alternating stress projected from syncope, p. 37); a Loup B statement, if ever written, would follow this method. Listed so the two records are not confused.

sources.note: Summarises Goddard 2012 (Loup B = Loup 4, 5, 6 recorded by Magon de Terlaye) and gives a vowel table drawn from Gustafson 2000 (Loup A); no statement on stress.

sources.citation: Goddard, Ives. 2016 [conference 2012]. The 'Loup' Languages of Western Massachusetts: The Dialectal Diversity of Southern New England Algonquian. Papers of the 44th Algonquian Conference, 104-138. Ottawa/Albany: SUNY Press. (Glottolog's only reference for loup1245.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress rule for Loup B. Only comparative remarks: 'The retention of word-final unstressed voiced syllables in Loup 3 and 4.. and Loup 6 makes these languages exceptional within SNEA' (p. 121); a Loup B word for 'cold' shows 'the syncope of the first vowel found in Abenaki' (p. 120). Describes the Loup B manuscript (pp. 105-106, n. 2) and argues it records three varieties (Loup 4, 5, 6).

sources.citation: Goddard, Ives. 2008. Notes on Mahican: Dialects, Sources, Phonemes, Enclitics, and Analogies. Papers of the 39th Algonquian Conference, 246-315.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Section 'Loup B' (pp. 248-249) describes the source as 'brief notes taken by François-Auguste Magon de Terlaye from refugees in Canada (Magon de Terlaye 1755; Goddard 1978b:71-72)' with r/l/n reflexes and doublets from more than one SNEA variety; nothing on Loup B stress. Stress/strong-weak-syllable remarks in the paper concern Mahican and Proto-Algonquian only (e.g. n. 13, p. 313: Mahican vowel-weakening rule; 'difficult to reconstruct the stress rules of Proto-Algonquian').

sources.citation: Costa, David J. 2007. The Dialectology of Southern New England Algonquian. Papers of the 38th Algonquian Conference, 81-127.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Loup B stress. p. 83 n. 1: 'The vocabulary known as "Loup B" contains data from at least two or three different languages and probably does not represent any dialect spoken in the SNEA language area. (See Goddard 1978:71-72.)' Loup B is otherwise only a comparison abbreviation (L B) in the data lists.

sources.citation: Gustafson, Holly. 1999. A Language on the Border: Identifying Nipmuck. Papers of the 30th Algonquian Conference, 122-128.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Loup A (Mathevet) only, no mention of Loup B. States that Nipmuck syncope of unstressed initial vowels 'provides internal evidence to the language's stress pattern, which seems to match the Proto-Algonquian alternating stress rule' (p. 124) — the same inference as Gustafson 2000 already recorded for loup1243.
